newsitem.title: USA: Connecticut turkey farmers are rare birds.
newsitem.headline: Connecticut turkey farmers are rare birds.

text.p: A few days before Thanksgiving, Carolyn Miller Stevens surveys a couple of dozen turkeys on her farm in this staid New England hamlet.
"They all would have gone to turkey heaven by now, except that a TV station wants to come by and film some," she said.
The stay of execution was understandable, since barnyard photo opportunities are increasingly rare in a state that once boasted all the trimmings of a thriving turkey industry.
Stevens, who owns Miller Foods Inc. with her sister, Sandi, raised just 400 birds this year -- a far cry from the days when her parents had a flock of 14,000 turkeys in 1962.
Even though Connecticut is part of the region that virtually invented Thanksgiving, its turkey industry has fallen on lean times.
Today there are only six turkey farms left in the state, down from 51 in 1949, state agriculture officials said.

"Most of the surviving ones are fairly small. The industry has been in a decline since the 1950s and '60s," said Gabe Moquin, the Connecticut Department of Agriculture's deputy director in the bureau of regulation and inspection.
The culprits are increasingly valuable real-estate in the land-scarce state, and higher costs of production.
The situation has ruffled the feathers of folks who want to put a homegrown bird on their Thanksgiving table.

"There's definitely a market for (Connecticut-grown turkeys)," said Rick Macsuga, lead marketing representative for the state Department of Agriculture. "Every year at this time, we get all kinds of calls from people looking for fresh birds, Connecticut-grown. Anybody who is raising birds is selling them, that's for sure."
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for fresh Connecticut turkeys, paying from $1.39 to $1.89 a pound.
There are no mass-producers of turkeys left in the state. One major producer, Grayledge Farms in Glastonbury, Conn., closed its operation in August.

Connecticut's turkey flock shrank to 15,000 birds this year from 25,000 last year and about 206,000 back in 1949, said Macsuga. The state's annual turkey production is valued at a lean $474,000, compared with $4.5 million in neighbouring Massachusetts, according to Moquin.
Because turkey production costs have gone up, the state's few surviving farmers have become more resourceful to feed the demand.

"For a Connecticut company to survive selling turkeys just once a year, you can't do it unless you are creative and diversify," said Stevens, whose 28-employee company spread its wings into transportation and food-broker businesses.
Turkeys account for just 10 percent to 12 percent of the company's revenues, she said.

In addition to the 400 birds raised on its six-acre farm, the company imports about 14,000 fresh turkeys a year from Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. This allows it to meet some of the demand without making the huge investment it would need for a federally inspected processing plant, Stevens said.
Orders come in as early as August, and usually trickle in right up to Thanksgiving day.
"We've UPS-ed turkeys to Kentucky and Boston, and we even have one customer from United Technologies who picks up his turkey and takes it with him on the Concorde to France," Stevens said.
